If mental health screenings for children without parental consent are controversial, it is because the conversation is missing nuance—not because the principle of informed consent is flawed.

---

🔹 Parental rights are foundational, yes. But so too is a child’s right to be safe—especially when abuse, neglect, or unaddressed trauma may stem from the very environment parental consent aims to protect.

🔹 The binary framing—either “consent always” or “intervention never”—fails to account for children in crisis, children in silence, and children with no advocate.

The real question is:

> Can we build a model that respects parental authority while preserving the ability to intervene when that authority is the source of harm?

---

We believe the answer lies in structured thresholds:

✅ Baseline screenings require parental opt-in.

🚨 Crisis response and life-threatening indicators bypass delay under tight oversight.

🛡️ All actions are logged, reviewed, and appealable.

---

This isn't an attack on parents—it's a defense of the voiceless.

Let’s not pretend this debate is simple. Children are not political abstractions. They are individuals caught between protection and permission—and that tension deserves more than slogans.
